Oof, tough market to compete in...

@Monad already has 4 established lending protocols accounting for ~$467M in active loans, mostly at variable rates.

So @BarterDeFi is entering into a market where they will have to compete with @Aave, @eulerfinance, or @Morpho – but I see a path how they could win.

In fact they have their moat and don't need to compete with Aave for general-purpose lending. Instead they can become the term-funding venue for a few large borrowing strategies.

If I were Barter, I’d look into:
• maturity-matched financing
• concentrated liquidity
• distribution via strategy operators
• predictable repayments

Overall, I’m glad to see them building toward retail products.
One of the few protocols I genuinely want to see succeed.

tweets.text:
This is basic stuff, but I feel like many emerging teams need a reminder.

Your paid ads are burning money if you:

1. Judge performance by ROAS alone.
2. Ignore a declining CTR when conversions remain stable.
3. Don’t investigate why a high CTR leads to fewer conversions.
4. Overlook rising CPMs when CTR stays flat.
5. Keep running ads as CTR and conversion rates decline.
6. Rarely test new creative concepts.
7. Ignore ad frequency and creative fatigue.
8. Make decisions based on a single bad day.
9. Don’t compare 7-day vs. 30-day performance trends.
10. Wait for ROAS to drop before investigating performance issues.

PS: In many cases, paid ads aren’t efficient at all.

So check your acquisition benchmarks against average customer acquisition costs by channel.

FYI: Paid ads are the most-used channel for teams at $50M+ ARR – because they CAN afford it.

A very sobering practice.

David Friedberg: Restricting Open Source AI is a Path to Tyranny

“Open source needs to be allowed and frankly encouraged to proliferate because the absence of that means that you're going to have tyrannical groups, ultimately, they become tyrannical.

They don't intend to be tyrannical, but every group that has the power to control what people see, what they're allowed to do, what they're allowed to access, how they're allowed to use things, what those specific weights are on ‘facts of history,’ on ‘proven science,’ on ‘the truth.’

That is where people become tyrannical because they have an opinion where they think they're right, and if they have the power, they will act on that opinion, and it will ultimately give them tyrannical force over a broader population.

That's what will happen if we limit the proliferation of open source software in AI.

And I've said it before, I'll say it again, ultimately, you can regulate, you can restrict, you can control, you can litigate, you can criminally penalize people for the outputs of what they use software to do.

But to limit software, to label software, to make it a point of restriction and control creates a regulated monopoly for the closed source products that are out there that ultimately, if aligned with certain government agencies, gives those government agencies and those individual corporations power and control over you, the individual, what you're allowed to do, what you're not allowed to do, and every business on Earth no longer operates freely.

None of us should want that. I don't care what your political affiliation is.”

Unfortunately, the # of headwinds facing Bitcoin continues to mount 

1) DATs unwinding

2) Prev miners now AI Neos selling BTC on their BS (Mara, etc.)

3) Saylor over-hang through STRC mechanisms (Future financing issues)

4) Quantum fears (whales who already got rich - why take the risk?) 

These ultimately dilute the digital gold narrative of Bitcoin and slows down potential flows. After all, any sane investor would just wait till the dust is settled to begin buying. 

As someone in the space, I wish for Bitcoin to succeed. But taking a long, hard, look at the current reality, and what we see is an asset cursed by what it has become. 

Option and perp flows outweighing spot buying is an issue because it signals that no one truly believes in it as they did in the past - when ownership falls, the asset becomes less like a real SoV, and more like a commodity-esque index used to measure and indicate volatility; not something that goes "up over time" as people had hoped 

As such, it is natural that the broader crypto market will start de-correlating with BTC.

thread_tweets.text:
Using our AgentX dataset as a rough estimate of the token mix corresponding to $44k in output, we arrive at an estimate of $125k all in.

It's impossible to say what the shape of this workload actually was. Alpöge describes working on this proof over the course of several weeks, so it's possible that the final proof was a small fraction of the total cost. 

On the other hand, in SemiAnalysis’s internal usage, we observe that human-in-the-loop work doesn't burn many tokens compared to asynchronous agentic work, which is what produced the proof. It’s therefore also possible that the two proof artifacts represent most of the total cost. (3/4)

thread_tweets.text:
The proof comprises two artifacts: a “book” that Alpöge has not released because it is “slop,” spanning 250k+ pages, and a Lean proof of 17.4M lines that is the current object of discussion.

We can estimate the number of tokens in the book based on Levent’s previous papers on arXiv, which average 1,946 tokens in the TeX source per page of output PDF using Anthropic’s newest tokenizer. This implies roughly 487M output tokens.

A randomly sampled 1.5% of the Lean averaged 35 tokens per line, which implies roughly 610M output tokens.

At Fable 5.2’s current price of $40/million output tokens, this comes out to $44k. (2/4)

thread_tweets.text:
The only Anthropic math result that discloses a token count was from August, when an Anthropic researcher told Claude, “Take a real stab at the Riemann hypothesis.” (That August result proved that at least 67.2% of nontrivial zeros lie on the critical line; Alpöge’s result today proves that it all of them do.)

Anthropic disclosed that Claude used 31M tokens in that effort, and the proof artifacts that it released totaled to around 3.3M. Thus, the overhead due to thinking and retrying on the way to a significant mathematical result can be estimated at around 89%.

This factor raises our previous cost estimate to $1.17M. 

This is more than the famous $1,000,000 prize that the Clay Mathematics Institute offers for solving the problem! (4/4)
